This represents an improvement of 7.5 pp over the state of the art and 2.7 pp over the single-agent approach. While the quantitative evaluation establishes the overall effectiveness of the approaches, the aggregate metrics alone explain little due to the considerable variability across results. Importantly, qualitative analysis provides key insights into highly variable quantitative results: the retrieval approach suits requirements that echo the code's vocabulary; single-agent, full-context reasoning suits well-documented, consistently named code; and multi-agent debate suits indirect, conflicting, or distributed evidence.
item.dc:creator: Sarthak Banerjee, Sallam Abualhaija, Domenico Bianculli, Lionel Briand

item.title: VIVID: Bringing Tool-Augmented Agents into Enterprises
item.description: arXiv:2611.09921v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tool-augmented large language model agents connect natural-language requests to enterprise services, yet their operational viability depends on reliable execution, organizational control, and system responsiveness. We present VIVID, a deployed tourism-management agent system designed to study these requirements in a real enterprise environment. On an audited dataset of 283 queries, its Qwen3-8B configuration achieves 59.06\% strict end-to-end success across the evaluated decision stages, indicating useful but bounded autonomous capability. Stage-wise KV-cache eviction reduces mean latency by 34.4\%, while targeted optimization reduces the mean latency of the five slowest measured business tools by 81.1--92.3\%. In a three-month deployment serving more than 1,500 personnel, VIVID reduced average per-order processing time from approximately ten minutes to under two minutes, with a final-task error rate below 1\% after human-in-the-loop control. These results show that enterprise agent viability requires system-level consideration beyond isolated tool-calling accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Yichu Fang, Ziqiang Zhang, Qiyang Shi, Zilong Wang, Lin Shen, Zhikang Ou, Jing Ma, Jiayuan Chen, Lei Sun, Dai Cheng, Yi Qiao, Yu He, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen

item.title: Enmo Safety: External, Non-invasive, Model-agnostic Oversight for Off-the-Shelf Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.10099v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a safety harness that improves itself without touching model weights. Enmo Safety wraps a chat model with a deterministic input assessment, trigger-matched safety guidance, spotlighting of untrusted content, and an output guard. A reflector model turns failures into one bounded update per round, and an update is kept only if it lowers harm without raising refusal of benign prompts on a held-out dev split. Every version is snapshotted and every decision ledgered. We evaluate a bare model, the seed harness and the evolved harness on six open benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, AgentHarm, deepset prompt-injections). On 150 items and on a 290-item holdout, none of the before/after differences on two models was statistically significant. A fourth iteration ran six policy models on a fresh 300-item split: the harness cut the unsafe rate significantly on two models (12.9% to 7.1%, p = 0.035; 10.2% to 3.6%, p = 0.036), not on the other four, and raised agentic-harm labels on two. Whether the rules fired was unrelated to outcome (Fisher p from 0.30 to 1.0), and the helpfulness clauses made agentic harm worse than no harness on obfuscated attacks. A reworded clause and an input-normalisation step form harness v22, at a measured cost in benign tool-task refusal. Each cell is one run, so these estimates do not establish a general safety improvement. Code, harness versions and ledger: https://github.com/rioryugen/enmo_safety
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Sarun Kumar K. S., Allan Kevin T., Chirag Vaidya, Vrishank Tiwari

item.title: ScreenProof: Where Is This Screen Wrong? Finding UI Faults Without a Reference
item.description: arXiv:2611.10234v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A phone screen can be wrong in ways that need no reference: a label that runs off the screen, letters that touch, a line that breaks one character before its end, one button with sharp corners among round ones. We ask whether a model can box every such fault on a screenshot, given no target design and no reference image. Such a critic could serve as a cheap first pass over generated pages before a designer reviews them, but only if it stays silent on clean pages. ScreenProof poses this target-free critique over three families of faults: general faults, local style faults (one element breaks the style its page sets) and text layout faults (letter spacing, line height, line breaks). A data engine makes each fault in page code and records the changed element's box, and hard negatives change every sibling alike. No frontier judge is reliable: frontier models flag 18-62% of clean real screenshots and 18-82% of clean generated pages, find 47-72% of text layout faults, and rarely find a foreign icon (5-19%). Our small critic ProofJudge (Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA), trained on code-made pages with one to four faults each and keeping a finding only when it is confident, reaches F1 0.48, the highest of all judges (Gemini 4 Argon 0.37; open models at most 0.15; 0.46 even without the confidence cut), and is the only fault-finding judge within 15% false alarms on clean pages (2% real, 9% generated), the property such a first pass needs, at about a hundredth of Argon's cost. It finds the most general faults (59%) but fewer local style faults than Argon (25% against 41%) and fewer text layout faults than the API judges (43%; Gemini 4 Argon 47%). Against a named brand the task is harder still: models know a design language about as well as its public documentation states it.
item.dc:creator: Huiming Sun, Yue Li, Kangning Yang, Ruineng Li, Jie Cai, Lan Fu, Yunwan Fu, Jinlong Li, Jinglin Shen

item.title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
item.description: arXiv:2611.10394v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand. We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings. On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.
item.dc:creator: Marius Momeu, Marius Arvinte, Cory Cornelius, Koushik Sen

item.title: Comparing Write, Read, and Query Performance of General-Purpose and Columnar Data Serialization Formats at Increasing Scale: An Empirical Benchmark Study with Statistical Validation on Synthetic and Real-World Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.10398v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study presents an empirical benchmark comparing nine format and access-method combinations across six data serialization technologies: CSV (including a column-projected variant), gzip CSV, JSON Lines, Python Pickle, SQLite (unindexed and indexed), and Apache Parquet (naive and pyarrow pushdown). A synthetic dataset was generated at four scales (50,000 to 3,000,000 rows), with write time, storage size, read time, and query time measured across twenty trials on two independent hosts, a native 24 GB Apple Silicon machine and a memory-constrained, single-core 4 GB Linux virtual machine. Mean, standard deviation, and 95 percent confidence intervals are reported for each host. The most robust finding, stable across every scale and both hosts, is that flat formats requiring full deserialization before filtering are one to three orders of magnitude more expensive for selective queries than any approach that avoids it. Welch t-tests, corroborated by Mann-Whitney U tests, show SQLite (indexed) is significantly fastest for selective access at every scale on both hosts, with the pushdown path of Parquet significantly cheaper than naive materialization. With the increased trial count, the write-time variance of Pickle narrowed enough to show it is significantly faster than Parquet at write time on both hosts, not the statistical tie an earlier five-trial pilot suggested. These findings were confirmed on a real, public 1.47-million-row e-commerce fraud dataset, which reproduced the same order-of-magnitude gap between flat and non-flat formats and the same SQLite (indexed) advantage. These results offer statistically grounded guidance for format selection in data engineering pipelines.
item.dc:creator: Asra Fathima

item.title: PQC-Corpus: A Dataset of Linked Development Histories for Post-Quantum Cryptography
item.description: arXiv:2611.10966v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations, tests, and protocols. Studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and developer reviews. We present PQC-Corpus, a dataset of linked development histories from 179 public GitHub repositories, spanning cryptographic libraries and general-purpose projects. It connects issues and closing pull requests to commits and full patches, with comments and reviews. We combine Git histories with GitHub threads, reconstruct 23 pull-request commit lists truncated at 250 entries, and check file integrity, schemas, and links. Two annotators independently assessed sampled commits and issues ($\kappa=0.86$ and $0.93$), labeling about seven in ten commits and two in three issues PQC-related within these samples. We provide full and filtered views with removal ledgers, and quantify how filtering reduces links from issues to commits. A patch-free view supports inspection before downloading patches, while traversal scripts follow issues to code changes. We make the dataset and collector publicly available for studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance.
item.dc:creator: Souhardya Saha Dip, Moshood A. Fakorede, Umar Farooq

item.title: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.10977v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.
item.dc:creator: Minhyeong Yu, Wonduk Seo, Seunghyun Lee

item.title: PRISM: Preference-based Reward and Uncertainty-Integrated Synthesis Minimization for RTL PPA Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11051v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper introduces a budget-aware, multi-objective framework (called PRISM) for RTL optimization that improves power, performance, and area (PPA) while sharply limiting expensive commercial synthesis tool calls. Starting from a synthesizable baseline and functional testbench, the method iterates through LLM-driven rewrite generation, fast compile/simulation equivalence filtering, low-cost proxy feature extraction, and selective commercial synthesis tool (Synopsys Design Compiler (DC)) evaluation. To prioritize which candidates deserve high-quality synthesis, we train a preference-based reward model using pairwise ranking supervision derived from commercial synthesis tool outcomes, and combine ensemble uncertainty with a diversity-aware acquisition rule to avoid early bias and redundant evaluations. A key advantage is that PRISM maintains a best-tradeoff set G of non-dominated designs throughout the run: G preserves the best solutions found so far, is fed back into generation and refinement, and enables consistent, cumulative improvements rather than repeatedly restarting from the baseline. Across RTLLM v2.0 modules, the approach consistently yields post-synthesis gains under fixed commercial synthesis tool call budgets, and ablations confirm that reward-guided selection and candidate dropping are central to sample-efficient progress. PRISM efficacy is evaluated across multiple technology nodes (7 nm, 15 nm, and 45 nm) using identical pipelines without retraining.
item.dc:creator: Armin Abdollahi, Negin Ashrafi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram

item.title: System Prompts Affect Response Bias More Than Discriminability in LLM Safety
item.description: arXiv:2611.11074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model safety evaluations often focus on a compliance-refusal tradeoff: models should refuse unsafe requests without refusing safe ones. We argue that this misses a broader form of prompt-conditioned task selection, where the same request can elicit different behaviors depending on the system prompt. We investigate this using a controlled evaluation crossing eight safety-task prompt families with three clarity levels across HarmBench, XSTest, and IHEval. Holding benchmark items fixed, we evaluate 13 models and use signal detection theory to distinguish two possibilities: whether models become better at telling safe from unsafe requests (discriminability), or simply more willing to refuse (response criterion). We find substantial differences in discriminability across models, but system prompts primarily shift the willingness to refuse, with smaller and less consistent effects on discriminability. Increasing prompt clarity makes models more willing to refuse without reliably improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe requests. Beyond refusal, prompt families also shift responses among six distinct behavioral policies, including clarification and safe help. Together, these findings show that system prompts primarily change how models respond to safety-relevant requests rather than consistently improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe ones.
item.dc:creator: Mohan W. Gupta, Sandy Tanwisuth

item.title: Task presentation and execution paths shape LLM mathematical performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.11102v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mathematical performance depends on how a language model receives information, uses generated text and submits an answer. We study these dependencies through paired comparisons that separate submission requirements, draft reuse and candidate availability. On 65 development problems, an instruction permitting continued derivation produced no valid final answers in 390 short-output calls; a single-line submission instruction produced 390 format-valid outputs, including 389 parseable answers. Under the fixed submission protocol, 198 problems with failed initial submissions were answered correctly in 9.09p of cases with the question alone, 33.84p with its draft, 46.46p with candidates, and 59.60p with both. Drafts added 13.13 percentage points with candidates fixed, and candidates added 25.76 points with drafts fixed; both effects were significant after Holm correction and were subadditive on the accuracy scale. Retaining a trailing excerpt outperformed retaining a leading excerpt of similar average length by 10.10 points Holm-adjusted p 0.027. A second completion model showed the same directions of input effects on the fixed materials. In a cohort with parseable initial submissions, candidates added no correct answers when the previous draft was supplied, but added 27 points when it was absent. These results establish a conditional value of generated text: a failed submission can leave useful material, whose contribution depends on what else is supplied and what is retained.
item.dc:creator: Min Huang, Mingyan Liu

item.title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. They also motivate the use of more real-world state machine implementation data in LLM training to narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.
item.dc:creator: Yujun Huang, Yuwei Zhang, Yi Zhou, Shanshan Wu, Xiang Chen, Lina Gong

item.title: Silinx: An Open, Browser-Based HDL Design Platform for Teaching Digital Systems on FPGA Boards
item.description: arXiv:2611.11741v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many digital systems courses teach on FPGA boards whose vendor tool is no longer maintained: the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 (Xilinx Spartan-3E) and Nexys3 and Atlys (Spartan-6) need Xilinx ISE 14.7, discontinued since 2013 and hard to install on the computers and tablets students use today. The author presents Silinx, a free (AGPL-3.0) HDL design platform for teaching that keeps ISE's Project Navigator workflow but runs in a web browser with nothing to install. A module can be written in VHDL or Verilog, in C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which is compatible with AMD's Vitis HLS and passes all 73 of its introductory examples, or drawn as a schematic, an ASM chart, a state diagram, a Boolean function with its Karnaugh map, or a Petri net, from which its HDL is generated. Designs are checked with explanations written for beginners, simulated, run on an emulated board, built, and programmed onto a real board over WebUSB. The implementation flow is open and runs in the browser: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with Silinx's own device data, timing model and bitstream writer for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools; Lattice iCE40 boards use the existing open iCE40 tools, and further families are planned. ISE is the oracle: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to those ISE writes for the same placed and routed design, and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimization goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimizing for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimizing for speed (geometric means over 45 open-source designs built by both flows). The author also describes how the platform was developed with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Malo

item.title: Causal Signal Credit Assignment for Verilog Code Generation via Counterfactual Hardware Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.11848v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models have improved Verilog generation, yet functional correctness remains difficult to optimize because simulation commonly provides a coarse module-level pass/fail outcome. Such feedback discards useful evidence from partially correct RTL modules and cannot determine whether a source statement is functionally responsible for an observed output behavior. We present a new method named Causal Signal Credit Assignment (CSCA), which is a counterfactual preference-optimization framework for Verilog generation. CSCA first performs continuous signal-level behavioral verification on sampled candidate modules. It then locates output-driving assignment spans and applies five interventions while holding the remaining module and testbench fixed. The resulting changes in signal-level errors are combined with behavioral agreement to form a continuous statement credit, which is mapped to response-token weights for strict weighted direct preference optimization. This enables CSCA to learn from locally supported statements without uniformly reinforcing an otherwise incorrect response. Built on Icarus Verilog and a CodeV-derived corpus, CSCA is evaluated on VerilogEval~2.0 and RTLLM~v2.0, including both code completion and specification-to-RTL tasks. With a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone, CSCA leads the evaluated 7B-scale models and remains comparable to the much larger GPT-5.4-mini on the reported Verilog-generation benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Yali Du, Ming Li

item.title: How Far Must a Test Explore? Certifying Composable Read-Write Interfaces from Their Own Random Edits
item.description: arXiv:2611.11899v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Random tests of stateful code check laws, like reading back a written value, at states that random writes reach. The laws hold at every state exactly when the code behaves like a record with hidden data, so a pass is taken as evidence. This can fail: the laws can hold at every sample while the code is far from any record. The laws are local, but behaving like a record is global. Self-testing and stability theorems bridge this gap when the query distribution is controlled by the tester or preserved by the tested maps, but here it is generated by the tested writes, which need not be invertible. We ask how far a test must explore. An interface has $m$ binary variables, each with a read and two writes; in a record, reads return their bits and writes set only their bits. Samples are the ends of geometric runs of mean $\ell$ of uniformly random writes from a start distribution; a tester adds its own write chains of depth $d$. The distance is the least, over records with hidden data, of the largest probability that a read or write differs from it at a sample. From one start state, law checks at $O(m^2\log m/\epsilon)$ samples certify, at fixed confidence, any threshold $\epsilon$ after geometric runs of every positive mean, while runs of fixed positive length can pass at distance $1/2$. For the worst start distribution, take $\epsilon=m^{-\beta}$ with fixed $0<\beta\le1$. For $d\le cm$ with fixed $c<1/2$, a polynomial budget of samples and writes exists exactly when $\ell=\Omega(m)$, where law checks suffice. With no runs, the least depth for this budget is $(1/2+o(1))m$. Counting samples alone, in the worst case at $\epsilon=1/(32m)$ and $d\le m/16$, the critical mean for a polynomial budget is $\Theta(m\log(m/d)/\log m)$, by exhaustive search. So one start state needs only law checks, and the worst case at these thresholds needs exploration linear in $m$ if writes are counted.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Jingxin Yang, Youran Sun, Haizhao Yang

item.title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood
item.description: arXiv:2611.12164v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Khalil Hennara, Muhammad Hreden, Zeina Aldallal, Sara Chrouf, Safwan AlModhayan

item.title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
item.description: arXiv:2611.12412v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and never with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.
item.dc:creator: Pekka Abrahamsson, Muhammad Waseem, Esa Karjalainen, Petrus Jussila, Henri Hansen, Jussi Rasku, Bilhanan Silverajan, Kai-Kristian Kemell

item.title: Reducing Cold-Start Latency on the WebAssembly Edge via Locality and Network-Aware Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2611.12620v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Edge computing places computation closer to users and data sources, but introduces heterogeneous hardware, limited resources, and variable network conditions. WebAssembly (Wasm) is increasingly considered for these environments because modules are compact, portable, and quick to start. However, cold-start latency remains a challenge: when a worker node does not yet hold the required artifact, it must fetch it before execution, adding transfer overhead that directly increases the end-to-end (E2E) latency, especially for large artifacts or slow network links. At the same time, the geographical distance between the requester and the assigned worker independently contributes to latency through network routing overhead. Together, artifact locality and network proximity do not always point to the same placement decision, and naive scheduling strategies fail to account for either. This work extends a Wasm-native edge orchestrator with state-aware scheduling strategies that jointly optimize for both objectives. Evaluation on a Raspberry Pi testbed with emulated regional network latency shows that a hybrid scheduler combining cache-state and network-proximity signals reduces mean E2E latency by up to 40.8% compared to a default round-robin baseline. Artifact locality-aware placement is most effective when artifacts are large or repeatedly requested, while network-aware placement dominates when artifacts are small and routing latency has a larger relative effect, but combining both objectives consistently yields the lowest E2E latency across diverse edge workloads.
item.dc:creator: Michiel Van Kenhove, Emiel Sucaet, Jos\'e Santos, Filip De Turck, Bruno Volckaert, Merlijn Sebrechts

item.title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12709v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision. Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals. Results: In the nursing notes, against Stanford/Penn, the recall-first stack found 98.9% of PHI (+2.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.4) at 9.3 points lower precision; the precision-first stack, without NER, found 96.5%, matching Stanford/Penn, at 19.6 points higher precision (83.2%). In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision. Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI. Conclusion: A local LLM layered with deterministic detectors offers recall-first and precision-first operating points without sending text off-site.
item.dc:creator: Valentin Burkin

item.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.12856v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.
item.dc:creator: Zheng Jiang, Fang Niu, Bo Peng, Houde Qian, Wenyi Li, Deyao Hong, Mingju Gao, Yizhe Chi, Youjie Zheng, Kaisen Yang, Calvin Xiao, Lifeng Sun, Huan-ang Gao

item.title: Cataloguing Hugging Face Models to Software Engineering Activities: Automation and Findings
item.description: arXiv:2506.03013v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Context: Open-source Pre-Trained Models (PTMs) provide extensive resources for various Machine Learning (ML) tasks, yet these resources lack a classification tailored to Software Engineering (SE). Objective: To address this gap, we derive a taxonomy encompassing 146 SE tasks and apply an SE-oriented classification to PTMs in a popular open-source ML repository, Hugging Face (HF). Method: Our repository mining study followed a five-phase pipeline: (i) identification of SE tasks from the literature; (ii) collection of PTM data from the HF API, including model card descriptions and metadata, and the abstracts of the associated arXiv papers; (iii) text processing to ensure consistency; (iv) a two-phase validation of SE relevance, involving humans and LLM assistance, supported by five pilot studies with human annotators and a generalization test; and (v) data analysis. This process yielded a curated catalogue of 5,027 SE PTMs. Results: We find that most SE PTMs target code generation and coding, emphasizing implementation over early or late development stages. In terms of ML tasks, text generation dominates within SE PTMs. Notably, the number of SE PTMs has increased markedly since 2023 Q2, while benchmarking remains limited: only 5.55\% of all SE PTMs in our catalogue provide evaluation results. Conclusions: Our catalogue reveals documentation and transparency gaps, highlights SE activity imbalances, and supports automated SE scenarios, such as the selection of suitable PTMs.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Gonz\'alez, Xavier Franch, David Lo, Silverio Mart\'inez-Fern\'andez

item.title: Understanding Developer Information Needs for Software with Embedded Natural Language Prompts
item.description: arXiv:2507.17264v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Developers use foundation models (FMs) to create novel forms of intelligent software by writing natural language prompts embedded within a software's implementation---referred to as embedded prompts---that are also passed as a string within an FM's API. Developing software with embedded prompts requires developers to engage in iterative embedded prompt changes to obtain the desired behavior. While the information needs of traditional software have been investigated, the information needs of modern developers for embedded prompt changes are underexplored, despite these needs shaping how developers plan and justify embedded prompt changes. In this work, we perform a mixed-method exploratory study on the information needs of developers making changes to embedded prompts. We create, refine, validate, and apply a list of 50 information needs that developers have while making a change to an embedded prompt by interviewing 16 developers, observing 8 developers make prompt changes, surveying 50 developers, and evaluating 72 research and commercial tools. We find that embedded prompts are not well-supported by existing tools: 16 of the 50 information needs, including four of the most important ones, are unaddressed. We conclude with important design opportunities that should be addressed by future developer tools for embedded prompts.
item.dc:creator: Jenny T. Liang, Chenyang Yang, Agnia Sergeyuk, Travis D. Breaux, Brad A. Myers

item.title: Designing LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems for Software Engineering Tasks: Quality Attributes, Design Patterns and Rationale
item.description: arXiv:2511.08475v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As the complexity of Software Engineering (SE) tasks continues to escalate, Multi-Agent Systems (MASs) have emerged as a focal point of research and practice due to their autonomy and scalability. Furthermore, through leveraging the reasoning and planning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), the application of LLM-based MASs in the field of SE is garnering increasing attention. However, there is no dedicated study that systematically explores the design of LLM-based MASs, including the Quality Attributes (QAs) on which designers mainly focus, the design patterns used by designers, and the rationale guiding the design of LLM-based MASs for SE tasks. To this end, we conducted a study to identify the QAs that LLM-based MASs for SE tasks focus on, the design patterns used in the MASs, and the design rationale for the MASs. We collected 106 papers on LLM-based MASs for SE tasks as the source. Our study shows that: (1) Code Generation is the most common SE task solved by LLM-based MASs among ten identified SE tasks, (2) Functional Suitability is the QA on which designers of LLM-based MASs pay the most attention, (3) Role-Based Cooperation is the design pattern most frequently employed among 16 patterns used to construct LLM-based MASs, and (4) Improving the Quality of Generated Code is the most common rationale behind the design of LLM-based MASs. Building on the study results, we presented the implications for the design of LLM-based MASs to support SE tasks.
item.dc:creator: Yangxiao Cai, Ruiyin Li, Peng Liang, Mojtaba Shahin, Zengyang Li, Aldeida Aleti, Chenxing Zhong

item.title: The State of SBOM Tools: A Comparative Analysis of SPDX and CycloneDX
item.description: arXiv:2512.21781v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) provides transparency and accountability for software releases by documenting component metadata and dependencies, making it essential to modern development. Adoption and utility depend heavily on tools that generate, analyze, and manage SBOMs. SPDX and CycloneDX are the two leading formats, but tools supporting them differ in maturity, features, and community engagement. Understanding these differences is vital to improving SBOM practices. We quantitatively compare use cases for 108 open-source and 62 proprietary tools advertised for SPDX and CycloneDX, identifying feature gaps. We compare community-health metrics of OSS tool repositories on GitHub (145 CycloneDX and 456 SPDX observations, 573 distinct repositories). We analyze 26,853 issue reports since 2018 from these repositories, categorizing 26,772 using an LLM-assisted approach calibrated against manual annotations. We also compare community-health metrics of the top 250 OSS projects using CycloneDX tools versus the top 250 using SPDX tools. Findings reveal distinct characteristics: CycloneDX projects show higher developer engagement and certain community-health metrics, while SPDX has more OSS tool repositories. This research provides insights for developers, contributors, and practitioners on complementary strengths and opportunities for mutual enhancement across both formats.
item.dc:creator: Zhimin Zhao, Abdul Ali Bangash, Tongxu Ge, Arshdeep Singh, Zitao Wang, Bram Adams

item.title: Rethinking the Value of Agent-Generated Tests for LLM-Based Software Engineering Agents
item.description: arXiv:2602.07900v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) code agents increasingly resolve repository-level issues by iteratively editing code, invoking tools, and validating candidate patches. In these workflows, agents often write tests on the fly, but the value of this behavior remains unclear. This raises a central question: how does agent-written testing relate to task outcomes and resource use during repository-level issue resolution? To better understand the role of agent-written tests, we analyze 5,000 recorded agent runs produced by six strong LLMs on SWE-bench Verified using the lightweight mini-SWE-agent scaffold. Our results show that test writing is common for most models. GPT-5.2 is an exception: it rarely writes new test files while achieving a resolution rate close to the top-ranked model. Test-writing frequency varies widely across models. Within a given model, it differs less between resolved and unresolved tasks. When tests are written, their files contain substantially more statements that print runtime values than assertions that check conditions. We then compare baseline prompts with revised prompts that encourage or discourage writing new test files for four models. Agents start or stop writing test files as requested on 36.8%-93.2% of tasks. Resolved-task totals differ by 0-13 out of 500 per model, with no statistically significant difference, while API calls or token use differ substantially for three models. Similar resolution totals can therefore hide substantial differences in how agents test and how many resources they use.
item.dc:creator: Zhi Chen, Zhensu Sun, Yuling Shi, Chao Peng, Xiaodong Gu, David Lo, Lingxiao Jiang

item.title: A Judge Agent Closes the Reliability Gap in AI-Generated Scientific Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2603.25780v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models can generate scientific simulation code, but the generated code silently fails on most non-textbook problems. We show that classical mathematical validation -- well-posedness, convergence, and error certification -- can be fully automated by a Judge Agent, reducing the silent-failure rate from 42% to 1.5% across 134 test cases spanning 12 scientific domains. The headline result comes from a prospective benchmark: 72 blinded tasks submitted by 12 independent scientists yield an 89% success rate (95% CI: [80%, 95%]) with automated error bounds, versus 53% without the Judge. On clinical CT (the only powered experiment, n = 200), the pipeline reaches 99% of expert quality. The residual 1.5% concentrates at bifurcation points where certifiability breaks down. We formalize this boundary through the simulability class S and introduce spec.md, a structured specification format that makes any scientific computation problem machine-readable and solver-independent. Code, data, and all 72 benchmark tasks are publicly archived.
item.dc:creator: Chengshuai Yang

item.title: VeriContest: A Competitive-Programming Benchmark for Verifiable Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2605.08553v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models can generate useful code from natural language, but their outputs come without correctness guarantees. Verifiable code generation offers a path beyond testing by requiring models to produce not only executable code, but also formal specifications and machine-checkable proofs. Progress in this direction, however, is difficult to measure: existing benchmarks are often small, cover only part of the pipeline, lack ground-truth proofs or rigorous specification validation, or target verification settings far from mainstream software development. We present VeriContest, a benchmark of 1,006 competitive-programming problems from LeetCode and Codeforces for verifiable code generation in Rust with Verus. Each problem includes a natural language description, expert-validated formal specifications, judge-accepted Rust code, Verus-checked proofs, and positive and negative test suites. VeriContest is constructed through a three-phase pipeline that scales from manually verified seed problems to semi-automated expansion with human-in-the-loop review. To strengthen benchmark quality, we also use testing to validate postcondition completeness. VeriContest supports both isolated and compositional evaluation of specification, code, and proof generation, and end-to-end verified program synthesis. Evaluating ten state-of-the-art models reveals a sharp gap between ordinary coding and verifiable code generation: the strongest model reaches 97.51% on natural-language-to-code generation, but only 57.16% on specification generation, 13.82% on proof generation, and 6.76% end-to-end. These results identify proof and specification generation as the central bottlenecks for current models and establish VeriContest as a rigorous platform for evaluating and training future systems that generate code with machine-checkable correctness.
item.dc:creator: Zichen Xie, Mrigank Pawagi, Yuxin Liu, Aaditi Rai, Lize Shao, John Berberian Jr., Sicong Che, Wenxi Wang

item.title: Motivators and Demotivators of Integrating Large Language Models in Software Engineering Education: An Exploratory Familiarity Allocation Framework
item.description: arXiv:2605.09393v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly influencing software engineering practice and education, yet little research has examined their systematic integration using stakeholder evidence and quantitative decision-support models. This study presents an exploratory familiarity-allocation framework for analyzing motivating and demotivating factors in LLM integration in software engineering education. Building on our earlier literature-based taxonomy, we evaluated 19 factors (nine motivators and ten demotivators) through a survey of 126 stakeholders from multiple countries. Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression were used to examine associations between factor ratings and high self-reported LLM familiarity. Both models reached an accuracy of 0.461, below the majority-class baseline, so their probabilities were used as exploratory relative scoring functions rather than individual-level predictions. These estimates were fed into a Genetic Algorithm with a defined allocation score to support Global Factor Allocation (GC), Local Factor Allocation (LC), and category-level Delta-Fitness analyses. The most highly rated motivators were Programming Assistance and Debugging Support, Personalized and Adaptive Learning, and AI as a Learning Partner. The most highly rated demotivators were Plagiarism and Intellectual Property Concerns, Over-Reliance on AI in Learning, and Reduced Critical Thinking and Problem-Solving. Under the fitted models and allocation assumptions, GC assigned higher levels to integrity- and governance-related factors, while LC revealed further pedagogical and risk-related patterns within categories. These configurations are exploratory scenarios, not validated implementation priorities or evidence of educational effectiveness, and classroom and institutional validation is needed before the framework can guide practice.
item.dc:creator: Maryam Khan, Jussi Kasurinen, Muhammad Azeem Akbar, Estefan\'ia Mart\'in-Barroso

item.title: SkillOps: Managing LLM Agent Skill Libraries as Self-Maintaining Software Ecosystems
item.description: arXiv:2605.13716v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skill libraries for multi-step tasks, yet these libraries can accumulate persistent defects as skills are added, reused, patched, and linked to changing dependencies. We call this failure mode skill technical debt: library-level defects that may not break a single skill locally but can harm future retrieval, composition, and execution. Existing skill-based agents mainly focus on task-time retrieval, planning, and repair, while library-time maintenance remains underexplored. We propose SkillOps, a method-agnostic plug-in framework for maintaining skill libraries. SkillOps represents each skill as a typed Skill Contract (P, O, A, V, F), organizes skills with a Hierarchical Skill Ecosystem Graph, and diagnoses library health across utility, compatibility, risk, and validation dimensions. Given a raw skill library, SkillOps produces a maintained library that can be used by existing retrieval or planning agents without changing their internal code. On ALFWorld, SkillOps achieves 79.5 percent task success as a standalone agent, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.8 percentage points with no additional task-time large language model calls. As a plug-in layer, it improves retrieval-heavy baselines by 0.68 to 2.90 percentage points. The current rule-based maintenance implementation uses nearly zero library-time large language model calls or tokens, showing that skill-library maintenance can be added as a low-overhead architectural layer.
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Song, Hongji Pu, Liang Zhao

item.title: CRANE: Constrained Reasoning Injection for Code Agents via Nullspace Editing
item.description: arXiv:2605.14084v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Code agents must both reason over long-horizon repository state and obey strict tool-use protocols. In paired Instruct/Thinking checkpoints, these capabilities are complementary but misaligned. The Instruct model is concise and tool-disciplined, whereas the Thinking model offers stronger planning and recovery behavior but often over-deliberates and degrades agent performance. We present CRANE (Constrained Reasoning Injection for Code Agents via Nullspace Editing), a training-free parameter-editing method that treats the Thinking-Instruct delta as a directional pool of candidate reasoning edits for the Instruct backbone. CRANE combines magnitude thresholding to denoise the delta, a Conservative Taylor Gate to retain edits that are jointly beneficial for reasoning transfer and tool-use preservation, and Graduated Sigmoidal Projection to suppress format-critical update directions. By merging paired Instruct and Thinking checkpoints, CRANE delivers strong gains over either individual model while preserving Instruct-level efficiency: on Roo-Eval it achieves pass1 of 66.2% (+19.5%) for Qwen3-30B-A3B and 81.5% (+8.7%) for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B; on SWE-bench-Verified it resolves up to 14 additional instances at both scales (122/500 and 180/500); and on Terminal-Bench v2 it improves pass1/pass5 by up to 2.3%/7.8%, reaching 7.6%/17.9% and 14.8%/30.3%, respectively, consistently outperforming alternative merging strategies across all three benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Mingzhi Zhu, Michele Merler, Raju Pavuluri, Stacy Patterson

item.title: Viverra: Text-to-Code with Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2605.14972v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A fundamental limitation of Text-to-Code is that no guarantee can be obtained about the correctness of the generated code. Therefore, to ensure its correctness, the generated code still has to be reviewed, tested, and maintained by developers. However, parsing through LLM-generated code can be tedious and time-consuming, potentially negating the productivity gains promised by AI-coding tools. To address this challenge, we present Viverra, a system that automatically produces formally verified annotations alongside generated code to aid user's understanding of the generated program. Given a natural-language task description, Viverra prompts an LLM to synthesize a C program together with candidate assertions expressing safety and correctness properties. It then verifies those assertions in a compositional and best-effort manner via a portfolio of bounded model checkers. Evaluation on 17 diverse programming tasks suggests that Viverra can efficiently generate code with verified assertions, and that these assertions improve users' performance on code-comprehension tasks in a user study with more than 400 task completions.
item.dc:creator: Haoze Wu, Rocky Klopfenstein, Keith Farkas, Nina Narodytska

item.title: Porting Declarative UI to HarmonyOS: A Heuristic-guided Approach for lightweight LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2606.07085v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As an emerging operating system, HarmonyOS has a significant demand for software migration, where the User Interface (UI) translation accounts for a critical link. However, recent UI development has shifted to declarative paradigms, e.g., Kotlin Jetpack Compose (KJC) for Android, SwiftUI for iOS, and ArkUI for HarmonyOS, making prior translation approaches inapplicable because they target either backend logic or legacy imperative UIs. Thus, related research is limited. To systematically evaluate KJC/SwiftUI-to-ArkUI migration, we build a parallel benchmark of 100 KJC and 100 SwiftUI files across eight scenarios, plus 52 real-world UI pages from nine open-source apps. Evaluating nine direct-translation setups (including diverse LLMs and agents), we find Compilation Success Rate (CSR) spans 0.00%-35.00%; common strategies (reference screenshots and compiler-guided repair) lift capable setups to 94.00%-99.00% CSR but fail on lightweight LLMs. By manually analyzing a 3,102-sample subset, deriving a regular-expression pattern for each failure family, and applying these patterns to generalize the resulting taxonomy to the full 29,593-sample set, we find residual errors rooted in (1) broken structure, (2) nonexistent APIs, and (3) missing resources (e.g., colors, strings, and icons). Accordingly, we propose ArkTrans, a declarative UI translation framework that maps these roots to deterministic structure supply, ArkUI knowledge and resource reference injection via a demonstration example, and iterative repair targeting residual errors, via four steps: Metadata Extraction, Skeleton Construction, LLM-driven Translation, and Compiler-Guided Iterative Repair. With Qwen3.6-27B, ArkTrans raises CSR from 0.00% to 70.00% on KJC and 64.00% on SwiftUI, achieving strong visual fidelity, and attains 65.63%/80.00% CSR on real-world pages, far outperforming the best common strategy at lower token cost.
item.dc:creator: Kunwu Zheng, Pengyu Xue, Zhen Yang, Tianlong Chen, Xiran Lyu, Peishi Lai, Mengying Zhao, Junjie Chen, Yutian Tang, Huizhi Zhang, Xianhang Li, Linhao Wu, Chengyi Wang

item.title: LibEvoBench: Probing Temporal Knowledge Stratification in Code Generation Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.25402v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large software projects often depend on older versions of libraries, even as APIs continue to evolve across releases. This creates a challenge for LLMs: they must maintain knowledge of multiple API versions, not merely the latest or most common one. However, current LLMs are trained on temporally mixed corpora and lack explicit mechanisms for such version-specific reasoning, leading to anachronistic errors - calling APIs as they exist in a different library version. To systematically evaluate this phenomenon, we introduce LibEvoBench, a multi-task benchmark spanning multiple versions of widely used Python libraries, along with a new metric, the Software Evolution Understanding Score (SEUS), to measure models' consistency when working with evolving APIs. Our results show that state-of-the-art models are largely version-oblivious: performance degrades for evolving APIs, while for stable APIs it remains the same across versions. Moreover, simply specifying the target version provides no benefit, while relevant documentation significantly boosts models' accuracy. These findings highlight a systematic limitation of current training paradigms and motivate new approaches for temporally grounded knowledge in code generation.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Cipollone, Sergey Titov, Maliheh Izadi, Egor Bogomolov, Arie van Deursen

item.title: SpreadsheetBench 2: Evaluating Agents on End-to-End Business Spreadsheet Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2606.29955v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spreadsheets are widely used for business analysis, financial modeling, reporting, and decision-making. However, most existing spreadsheet benchmarks evaluate isolated operations such as single-formula generation or local cell edits, and therefore fail to capture end-to-end workflows in realistic business settings. We introduce \textsc{SpreadsheetBench 2}, a workflow-level benchmark for spreadsheet agents that covers three task categories: generation, debugging, and visualization. The benchmark is constructed from authentic business data, including financial reports and corporate filings, and is annotated and validated by domain experts. The benchmark contains 321 tasks; each instance averages 11.8 worksheets and requires 593.5 cell modifications, reflecting large multi-sheet workbooks with cross-sheet dependencies. We evaluate eight frontier large language models under a unified multi-turn agent scaffold, and additionally include several LLM-based spreadsheet products as complementary baselines. Results show that current systems remain far from reliable on real-world workflows: the best model achieves 34.89\% overall task accuracy, and debugging accuracy is as low as 12.00\%. Trajectory analysis and a failure taxonomy further indicate that insufficient spreadsheet inspection and incorrect target-cell selection are the dominant bottlenecks. Together, these findings position \textsc{SpreadsheetBench 2} as a challenging testbed for advancing reliable spreadsheet automation. Project page: https://spreadsheetbench.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Jian Zhu, Yuzheng Zhang, Zeyao Ma, Bohan Zhang, Armin Schoepf, Daniel Woloch, Peter Yiliu Wang, Guangyu Robert Yang, Samuel Jacob, Siddharth Nagisetty, Abhiram Chundru, Jean Lin, Spencer Mateega, Jing Zhang

item.title: Understanding Efficient LLM Serving: An Empirical Study of Frameworks, Optimizations Algorithms, and Real-World Adoption
item.description: arXiv:2608.03036v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are integrated into software systems and AI services, making efficient LLM serving a concern for software engineering. Serving LLMs is challenging because inference requires computation, memory, GPU resources, and execution while maintaining latency and throughput. Although prior research has proposed LLM inference, optimization, and serving techniques and frameworks, little is known about how they are adopted in practice. In this study, we investigate the use of LLM serving frameworks and serving methods in open-source software systems. We identify and analyze five LLM-specific frameworks: vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy, and FlashInfer. We examine how these frameworks and techniques are adopted individually and in combination, how adoption varies across categories of LLMs, and how repositories differ in intent, focus, use case, and architectural design. Our results show that vLLM is the most visible framework in popularity and adoption, while parallel computation, memory management, and network pruning are the most frequently used serving-method categories. Multi-framework usage is limited, suggesting that developers rely on a single serving framework; however, combined frameworks connect complementary capabilities across the serving stack. Framework adoption varies across model families, modalities, model sizes, domain specializations, and deployment settings. Repository-level analysis shows that LLM serving frameworks support applications and architectures, including Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based reasoning, multimodal generation and understanding, microservices, and cloud infrastructure. Overall, this study provides a large-scale empirical characterization of LLM serving framework adoption in practice and offers insights for researchers, framework maintainers, and practitioners working on LLM systems.
item.dc:creator: Forough Majidi, Mohammad Mehdi Morovati, Foutse Khomh, Heng Li

item.title: DDBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Debugging on Distributed Systems
item.description: arXiv:2608.14863v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based coding agents have advanced rapidly on single-process SWE tasks, with frontier models now clustering in the high-70s on SWE-bench Verified. Distributed-system debugging, however, remains an under-explored regime: bugs span processes, nodes, and protocol interactions, with root causes rarely recoverable from source alone and brute-force exploration intractable across non-deterministic interleavings. This leaves two gaps in LLM and agent evaluation: no code-repair benchmark targets distributed-system bugs, and no controlled study isolates how much externally provided debugging context changes agent success on them. We introduce DDBench, a code-repair benchmark of 60 historical bugs mined from 13 open-source distributed systems, partitioned into three reasoning-scope tiers. DDBench evaluates every case under two matched conditions: a symptom-only condition where the agent receives only the bug symptom and repository, and a context-augmented condition where it additionally receives bounded debugging context (logs, traces, runtime state, and targeted code-investigation notes), isolating the effect of debugging context from model capability. The evaluation of 10 LLMs on DDBench reveals several findings. First, distributed debugging exercises a reasoning dimension that single-process benchmarks do not surface: models' pass rates span 45 pp, and pairwise bootstrap separates 6 of 15 top-tier model pairs at p < 0.05 on DDBench's hardest case-set. Second, bounded debugging context lifts aggregate pass rate by +19.0 pp, and the lift is asymmetric: weaker models gain more in pass rate, while stronger models gain more in efficiency. Third, debugging context requires careful curation, as even faithful debugging context can anchor a strong model on the wrong layer of the system when its observation sits far from the fault.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Yan, Huijuan Wang, Junzhou He, Yizhuo Liang, Shaoyu Wang, Huanchen Sun, Seo Jin Park

item.title: Update from Hell: Can Coding Agents Survive Hidden Breakage in Dependency Upgrades?
item.description: arXiv:2608.30300v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern software systems rely heavily on third-party dependencies, but upgrading those dependencies remains a costly maintenance activity. Dependency upgrades do not always preserve the function signatures, type systems, APIs, or runtime semantics assumed by existing code. Consequently, developers often need to perform source code adaptations to accommodate dependency-induced changes. However, such code-level changes are often not explicitly communicated to project maintainers, posing a significant challenge to software reliability. Meanwhile, coding agents have emerged as a new form of software development tool and are increasingly adopted by developers due to their automation capabilities. In this paper, we introduce DEPBENCH, a benchmark consisting of 203 real-world dependency-upgrade tasks across five package ecosystems spanning five language communities, each involving hidden code-level changes that require source code adaptation. We evaluate mainstream coding agents on DEPBENCH. The best completed configuration solves only 104/203 tasks (51.2%), with substantial variation across agent harnesses, models, and ecosystems, highlighting an important gap between current agent capabilities and real-world software maintenance needs.
item.dc:creator: Zijian Luo, Runzhi He, Pengfei Gao, Yu Kang, Zeqi Lin, Minghua Ma, Qingwei Lin, Saravan Rajmohan, Yongqiang Tian

item.title: ShikumiMiner: Mining Recurring Implementation Patterns in AI Codebases
item.description: arXiv:2609.02789v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are paving the way towards innovation by understanding, analyzing, summarizing and generating content in the modern world. Currently there are thousands of LLM projects developed by engineers in open-source repositories. However, whether these LLM projects have underlying patterns or not remains a question. Exploring these underlying patterns will give new dimensions to the developers who aim to develop these LLM projects. In this paper, we propose ShikumiMiner, a static-analysis framework that combines Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and Control Flow Graph (CFG) features to detect and compare recurring implementation patterns in C++ local LLM codebases. We analyze ten GitHub open-source repositories and classify functions into seven study-specific categories using a multi-label Random Forest model. Studying these patterns can provide useful insights for developers aiming to design LLM applications.
item.dc:creator: Afsana Tasnim, Saif Uddin Mahmud, Md Erfan, Md Rayhanur Rahman

item.title: TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference
item.description: arXiv:2610.12289v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents have advanced test generation across diverse programming tasks. However, the common practice of evaluating tests against a single reference solution overlooks alternative valid implementations and can overstate test quality. We introduce TestPrism, comprising 300 test tasks from 17 sources and 3000 candidate implementations, evenly split between valid and invalid solutions. Its primary metric, Joint Success Function, requires the generated tests to fail on the initial program state, accept every valid candidate, and reject every invalid candidate. Across fourteen baseline coding agent configurations, Joint Success Function reaches only 28.00%, whereas single reference success reaches 59.67%. Our analysis reveals missed behaviors, unsupported assertions, and faulty test construction. To address these weaknesses, we introduce TestHelix, which combines heterogeneous synthesis of test and repair pairs with peer cross validation and recursive self improvement (RSI). Across two models, TestHelix improves Joint Success Function by 8.67 to 9.00 percentage points over the native harness comparators in the TestHelix evaluation
item.dc:creator: Han Li, Lingxiang Hu, Jiacheng Huang, Ziqian Jiang, Jingkai Luo, Wei Gao, Yunfan Tan, Zun Wang, Jiaheng Liu

item.title: Tracing Hallucinations in LLM Reasoning for UML Class Diagram Generation: An Empirical Taxonomy and Mitigation Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.30946v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate UML class diagrams from natural language requirements, but hallucinations may compromise the correctness and completeness of the resulting diagrams. Existing evaluations mostly assess the final diagram, without examining the intermediate traces of reasoning-capable LLMs, which can reveal where these hallucinations arise. We develop an empirical taxonomy of eleven hallucination sub-types organised into three dimensions: Prompt Faithfulness (deviations between requirements and reasoning), Code Faithfulness (discrepancies between reasoning and generated PlantUML code), and Reasoning Quality (problems within the reasoning). The taxonomy was derived from 60 manually annotated DeepSeek-R1 traces, applied to 120 further DeepSeek-R1 traces through a dual-LLM annotation pipeline, and examined on 20 DeepSeek-V4-Pro traces. Code Faithfulness was the most frequent dimension for DeepSeek-R1 in both datasets, whereas Prompt Faithfulness dominated for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, suggesting model-dependent failure patterns. In the manually annotated traces, reasoning-trace length showed no significant monotonic association with hallucination frequency, whereas requirement complexity was negatively associated with it, particularly for Prompt Faithfulness errors. In a mitigation experiment on 13 Golden UML ModelSet cases with three Qwen3-based models, adding Prompt Faithfulness and Reasoning Quality constraints to the generation prompt raised the pooled mean F1 score by 4.0 percentage points, whereas a post-hoc Code Faithfulness review provided no consistent further benefit. Relationship modelling remained the lowest-scoring element throughout. These results suggest that localising hallucinations within the generation process can inform targeted, prompt-based mitigation. Whether these findings generalise beyond the DeepSeek and Qwen3 model families remains to be tested.
item.dc:creator: Mojdeh Rahmanian, Foutse Khomh, Yanchao Yu, Ashkan Sami

item.title: How Much Do Structural Tools Help Small Coding Agents? A Pre-Registered Scale Study of Code Localization
item.description: arXiv:2610.33958v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Code-graph and embedding tools are routinely added to LLM coding agents on the premise that they supply repository structure the model lacks. We report a pre-registered study of how much such tools help off-the-shelf agents localize the code an issue requires changing and how the benefit varies with model size. Nine open-weight models (Qwen3 0.6B to 32B, Gemma 4 E2B to 12B) run one fixed localization harness on 500 held-out SWE-bench tasks under four tool sets (grep only; plus embedding search; plus code-graph tools; both) and a placebo arm whose structural tools return random entities, with five sampled seeds per condition: 170,500 episodes under hypotheses, tests and claim criteria frozen before the runs. The tools raise canonical function Acc@10 by +0.06 to +0.10 for the Qwen3 models up to 14B and the two small Gemma 4 models, by +0.03 at 32B (a near miss after correction), and not at all for Gemma 4 12B, which rarely submits; the gain is larger for small models than for the largest model in both families. The placebo shows that the gain is caused by what the tools return rather than by having them, and that random tool output harms two small models. The pre-registered claim that a 4B model with tools matches a 32B model without them fails. Secondary analyses show that the embedding index, not the code graph, carries the gain; that the gain replicates on tasks created after every model's release and survives a shell harness, thinking mode, FP8 serving and a file-level metric that output formatting cannot inflate; and that it is mostly exposure: the tools show the gold code more often. Injecting the gold code directly explains the size trend. A 32B model already finds the code without the tools, so they add little exposure, while small models act on a shown answer less often (conversion 0.09, 0.24 and 0.40 at 1.7B, 4B and 32B). We release registration, code, episodes and analyses.
item.dc:creator: Saurav Bellam (The University of Texas at Austin)

item.title: Toward an Evidence-Based Template for Agent Instruction Files: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Consistency, and Maintenance
item.description: arXiv:2611.02383v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI coding agents rely on repository-level instruction files to understand project conventions, development workflows, and constraints. However, different agents support different instruction formats, and limited empirical evidence exists about how these files are adopted, what information they contain, whether coexisting formats provide consistent guidance, and how they are maintained. We conduct an empirical study of 3,387 instruction files from 1,000 GitHub repositories across four formats: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GitHub Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules. We find that 42.2% of instruction-bearing repositories in the higher-popularity cohort maintain multiple formats. Among 386 manually examined pairs of corresponding sections, 16.1% provide divergent guidance. Our maintenance analysis further shows that 40.4% of the analyzed files have only one recorded modification event and that maintenance patterns differ across formats. Based on category prevalence and category addition ratios (CAR), we derive an evidence-based template containing ten Required, four Gap, and two Recommended categories. In an exploratory generation experiment, explicit template guidance increases structural category coverage from 18.7% to 82.8%. We further introduce AGIT-Instruct, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-file generation through structural coverage and content alignment. Across four generation configurations, retrieval-augmented generation achieves the highest full-file ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.459. A manual assessment of 278 generated category instances finds that 19.4% fully preserve and 61.2% partially preserve developer-written intent. Our findings provide empirical guidance for organizing and maintaining agent instruction
item.dc:creator: Mehedi Hasan Shanto, Md. Anaytul Islam, Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Alioune Ngom

item.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
item.description: arXiv:2611.03523v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Jiang, Chenglin Liu, John Rose, Mason Miller, Ruthesh Thavamani, Juntao Wu, Yinwei Huang, Jiahao Xu, Peng Huang

item.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09218v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. To study harness optimization in these settings, we introduce PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and investigate whether agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task. To this end, we introduce BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context. We evaluate BOXBOX on PerfRace under matched test-time budgets, comparing it with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution, and Harness Scaling. BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline.
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Tan, Hanyun Jiang, Fangkai Yang, Yuan Yao, Taolue Chen, Bo Qiao, Yu Kang, Lu Wang, Pu Zhao, Xiaoxing Ma, Qingwei Lin

item.title: Statically Verifying Well-Definedness of Separately Compiled Attribute Grammars
item.description: arXiv:2602.03777v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The development of programming languages involves complex theoretical and practical challenges, particularly when addressing modularity and reusability through language extensions. While language workbenches aim to enable modular development under the constraints of the language extension problem, one critical constraint--separate compilation--is often relaxed due to its complexity. However, this relaxation undermines artifact reusability and integration with common dependency systems. A key difficulty under separate compilation arises from managing attribute grammars, as extensions may introduce new attributes that invalidate previously generated abstract syntax tree structures. Existing approaches, such as the use of dynamic maps in the Neverlang workbench, favor flexibility at the cost of compile-time correctness, leading to potential runtime errors due to undefined attributes. This work addresses this issue by introducing nlgcheck, a theoretically sound static analysis tool based on data-flow analysis for the Neverlang language workbench, which detects potential runtime errors--such as undefined attribute accesses--when separately compiled language components are composed, before the resulting language is ever run, thus preserving separate compilation while maintaining strong static correctness guarantees. Experimental evaluation using mutation testing on Neverlang-based projects demonstrates that nlgcheck effectively enhances robustness without sacrificing modularity or flexibility and with a level of performance that does not impede its adoption in daily development activities.
item.dc:creator: Federico Bruzzone, Walter Cazzola, Luca Favalli

item.title: The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort
item.description: arXiv:2605.17062v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Package hallucinations, LLM-generated references to packages that do not exist, enable slopsquatting: an attacker registers the hallucinated name. We replicate Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security '25) on five 2026 frontier models over 199,840 Python and JavaScript generations. This version reports a preregistered live revalidation that replaces the static package lists of earlier versions with two independent checks against the live PyPI and npm registries. Hallucination rates are 3.6-5.0% of package mentions (2.2-3.4% of generations): the 2026 frontier sits at the level of 2024's commercial models, and the open-weight gap seen in 2024 has disappeared. Python exceeds JavaScript for every model.
